mainTopic: How much of the court must agree to a mistaken ruling, the judges' shared responsibility, and the laws of acting on a reversed ruling or a ruling that uproots a whole מצוה.
overview: This amud opens by closing a question from the previous amud with תיקו. Next, רבי יונתן teaches that a court brings its offering only if every judge agreed to the mistaken ruling, and רב הונא בריה דרב הושעיא supports this from the word 'כל'. The גמרא defends רבי יונתן against two משניות by saying the judge who disagreed nodded along. רב משרשיא then refutes him from the פסוק 'הגוי כלו', which follows the majority, so 'כל עדת' is reinterpreted to mean that the whole court must be present. רבי יהושע teaches that every judge, even a student before his teacher, shares the blame, and רב הונא and רב אשי brought others in to share that weight. A new משנה discusses someone who acted on a ruling the court had already reversed, and it teaches that uprooting a whole מצוה is פטור while cancelling one detail is חייב. The גמרא explains רבי שמעון's exemption, answers a challenge about collecting money for the offerings, and ends with רבי זירא comparing רבי אלעזר's view to eating fat that might be חלב.

steps.title: The second side of the question: must the same court become aware?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes an open question. Perhaps the offering requires that the very court that gave the ruling be the one to realize the mistake.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or perhaps we need the awareness of that same court that gave the ruling.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a question it started earlier. Here it gives the second possible answer: maybe only the original court's own realization counts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first side, from before this section, held that the realization need not come from the original court that ruled. This second side says the realization must come from the same court that ruled. If so, once that court is gone, no offering would be brought.

keyTerms.meaning: Or perhaps: brings in the other side of a question
Awareness, realizing that a mistake was made
We require
They ruled, gave a halachic ruling

phrases.english: Or perhaps the awareness
phrases.notes: The word in square brackets is added in the corrected wording to make the sentence complete.

phrases.english: of that same court that ruled is what we require!

steps.triggerLanguage: אוֹ דִּלְמָא יְדִיעָה דְּהָהוּא בֵּית דִּין דְּהוֹרוּ בָּעִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the second side of a question that began before this section.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the realization of the mistake must come from the same court that issued the ruling.

steps.title: The question is left unresolved
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא cannot decide the question, so it says תיקו: it stays open.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא admits it has no proof either way and leaves the question open.
steps.deeperAnalysis: תיקו means no source settles the question. Neither side is proven, so the question about whose awareness counts stays undecided.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it stand: the question remains unresolved

steps.whatToRemember: Whether the original court must be the one to realize its mistake is left as a תיקו.

phrases.english: Let it stand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the question raised in step 1 without an answer.

steps.title: All the judges must agree to the ruling
steps.stepSummary: רבי יונתן teaches that even if a hundred judges sat, they are not obligated in the offering unless all of them gave the ruling. He learns this from the words 'כל עדת ישראל'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יונתן said: If a hundred judges sat to rule, they are not obligated until all of them rule, as it says: 'And if the whole assembly of Israel errs.' That means until all of them err, until the ruling spreads through the whole assembly of Israel.
steps.whatsHappening: A new teaching begins. רבי יונתן says the court's offering applies only when every judge agrees to the mistaken ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says 'כל עדת ישראל', 'the whole assembly'. רבי יונתן reads 'whole' literally: every member of the court must share the ruling. A majority is not enough here, even in a very large court.

keyTerms.meaning: To issue a halachic ruling
Obligated, here in bringing an offering
The assembly of Israel, read here as the court
They err by mistake
Spreads out

steps.whyThisMatters: This rule sets up the challenges from the משנה in steps 6 and 8, and רב משרשיא's refutation in steps 10-12.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yonatan said:
A hundred who sat to give a ruling
are not obligated until all of them rule,
as it is said:
"And if the whole assembly of Israel errs"
meaning, until all of them err,
until the ruling spreads
through the whole assembly of Israel.
phrases.notes: The words in square brackets are added in the corrected wording. Some versions don't have them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new topic after the תיקו.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Judges bring the offering only if every one of them agreed to the mistaken ruling.

steps.title: Logical support: 'all' must mean truly all
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא בריה דרב הושעיא supports רבי יונתן. The Torah usually treats a majority like the whole, so writing 'all' here must mean every single judge, even a hundred.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא son of רב הושעיא said: This also makes sense. Throughout the whole Torah we hold that the majority counts like the whole. Yet here it is written 'the whole assembly'. Since that is so, all must agree, even if they are a hundred.
steps.whatsHappening: Another אמורא backs up רבי יונתן with reasoning. He explains why the word 'כל' must be taken literally.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally רובו ככולו applies, so a majority would have counted anyway. If the Torah still chose to write 'כל', it must be teaching something new: that here a majority is not enough. So even in a court of a hundred, all must agree.

keyTerms.meaning: So too it makes sense: introduces supporting logic
We hold, we have an established rule
The majority of something counts like all of it
Since this is so

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think רב הונא is using רובו ככולו to say a majority is enough. He says the opposite: since a majority usually counts anyway, the extra word 'כל' must demand everyone.
steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי יונתן and רב הונא בריה דרב הושעיא, a majority is not enough for the court's offering, and every judge must agree. This view is refuted in step 12.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב הוֹשַׁעְיָא:
phrases.english: Rav Huna son of Rav Hoshaya said:
So too it is logical,
for throughout the entire Torah we hold
that its majority is like all of it,
and here it is written "the whole assembly".
Since that is so, all must agree, even if they are a hundred.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב הוֹשַׁעְיָא הָכִי נָמֵי מִסְתַּבְּרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבי יונתן's reading of the פסוק with logic.
steps.raayaObject: רבי יונתן's rule that every judge must agree.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The general principle רובו ככולו, which makes the word 'כל' look extra unless it means everyone.

steps.title: Quoting the משנה about a judge who knew the ruling was wrong
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes our משנה. A judge or qualified student who knew the court was wrong but still followed it must bring his own offering, because he did not rely on the court.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned: The court ruled, and one of them knew they were mistaken, or a student fit to rule knew. He went and acted according to their ruling. Whether they acted and he acted with them, or they acted and he acted after them, or they did not act and he acted, he is obligated, because he did not rely on the court.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is bringing a source to test רבי יונתן's rule. This step sets up the challenge that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says someone who knows the הלכה but follows a wrong ruling anyway is personally obligated. He knew better, so he cannot blame the court. The detail that one judge disagreed is what the גמרא will use against רבי יונתן.

keyTerms.meaning: Qualified to give halachic rulings
According to their word, based on their ruling
Relied on the court

phrases.english: We learned:
phrases.notes: The word in square brackets is added in the corrected wording. It tells us a משנה is being quoted.

phrases.english: The court ruled,
and one of them knew that they erred,
or a student who is fit to rule knew it,
and he went and acted according to their ruling,
whether they acted and he acted with them,
or they acted and he acted after them,
or they did not act and he acted,
he is obligated,
because he did not rely on the court.

steps.triggerLanguage: תְּנַן הוֹרוּ בֵּית דִּין וְיָדַע אֶחָד מֵהֶן שֶׁטָּעוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a משנה to test רבי יונתן's rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A judge or qualified student who knows the ruling is wrong but follows it is personally obligated, because he did not rely on the court.

steps.title: Challenge: other people are exempt even though one judge disagreed
steps.stepSummary: The משנה suggests that only the judge who knew is obligated, while others are exempt because they relied on the court. But if one judge disagreed, the ruling was not unanimous, so according to רבי יונתן it should not count as a court ruling at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: This one is obligated, which means someone else is exempt. But why? The ruling was not complete!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא makes an inference from the משנה and uses it to challenge רבי יונתן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the משנה says this person is obligated, ordinary people who followed the ruling must be exempt. An ordinary person is exempt only if the ruling counts as a real court ruling. But רבי יונתן says a ruling counts only if all agreed, and here one judge disagreed.

keyTerms.meaning: Exempt
But why?
The ruling was completed, fully agreed upon

phrases.english: It is this one who is obligated,
which means another person is exempt.
But why?
The ruling was not completed!

steps.triggerLanguage: הַאי הוּא דְּחַיָּיב הָא אַחֵר פָּטוּר וְאַמַּאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the משנה from step 5 to attack רבי יונתן's rule from step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יונתן's rule that a ruling counts only if all the judges agreed.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה exempts ordinary people who followed the ruling, so it treats the ruling as valid. Yet one judge disagreed, so the ruling should not count under רבי יונתן's rule.

steps.title: Answer: the dissenting judge nodded in agreement
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the משנה's case is one where the judge who knew the truth nodded his head along with the others. So the ruling was unanimous on the outside.
steps.simpleTranslation: What are we dealing with here? A case where that one judge nodded his head.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבי יונתן by explaining the exact case of the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though this judge knew inside that the ruling was wrong, he showed agreement by nodding. So the ruling was formally agreed by all, and it counts as a complete court ruling. Others who relied on it are exempt, but he himself is obligated because he knew the truth.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? Narrows the case to answer a challenge
Nodded his head, showing agreement

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יונתן's rule stands. In the משנה, the judge who knew better nodded along, so the ruling still counts as agreed by all.

phrases.english: What are we dealing with here?

phrases.aramaic: כְּגוֹן שֶׁהִרְכִּין הַהוּא אֶחָד מֵהֶן בְּרֹאשׁוֹ.
phrases.english: A case where that one of them nodded his head.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 6.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought the knowing judge openly disagreed, so the ruling was not unanimous.
steps.terutzMaskana: He nodded in agreement, so the ruling was formally unanimous, and רבי יונתן's rule fits the משנה.

steps.title: A second משנה: the silent judge
steps.stepSummary: A משנה says that if one judge protested 'You are mistaken,' the court is exempt. This suggests that if he stayed silent, they are liable, even though not all of them ruled. That goes against רבי יונתן.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: If the court ruled, and one judge knew they were wrong and told them 'You are mistaken,' they are exempt. So the only reason they are exempt is that he spoke up. If he had just stayed quiet, they would be liable and the ruling would be complete. But why? Not all of them ruled!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another משנה to challenge רבי יונתן. It shows that a ruling can count even when one judge did not truly agree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה exempts the court only because the judge said out loud 'You are mistaken.' From this we learn that if he was silent, the court is liable. But a silent judge who knew the truth did not really join the ruling, so according to רבי יונתן it should not count.

keyTerms.meaning: You are mistaken
Exempt (here, from bringing the offering)
Liable, obligated
He simply stayed silent

phrases.english: Come and hear: The court issued a ruling,
and one of them knew that they had erred
and he said to them, "You are mistaken"
these are exempt.
The reason they are exempt is that he said to them "You are mistaken,"
but if he had simply stayed silent, they would be liable,
and the ruling would be complete.
But why? Not all of them issued the ruling!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After defending רבי יונתן in step 7, the גמרא brings a second משנה with a similar problem.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יונתן's rule that every judge must join the ruling
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה implies that a silent judge who knew the truth does not stop the ruling from counting, so not every judge truly has to agree.

steps.title: Same answer: he nodded his head
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers as before: the silent judge nodded along, so on the outside everyone agreed.
steps.simpleTranslation: They say: Here too, it is a case where he nodded his head.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers this challenge with the same answer it gave in step 7.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Silent' in this משנה means he did not protest, and he even nodded with the others. So the ruling looked unanimous, and רבי יונתן's rule is kept.

keyTerms.meaning: So too, here as well
He nodded (bowed) his head in agreement

phrases.english: They say: So too here,
it is a case where he nodded his head.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי: הָכִי נָמֵי כְּגוֹן שֶׁהִרְכִּין בְּרֹאשׁוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case: the silent judge actually nodded along
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A silent judge did not join the ruling, so it was not unanimous.
steps.terutzMaskana: The silent judge nodded, so the ruling was unanimous on the outside, as רבי יונתן requires.

steps.title: רב משרשיא's objection: decrees on the community
steps.stepSummary: רב משרשיא brings a ברייתא: a גזירה may be made only if most of the ציבור can keep it. This sets up a proof that 'whole' can mean 'most'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב משרשיא objects: Our Sages relied on the words of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל and רבי אלעזר ברבי צדוק, who said: We do not make a decree on the community unless most of the community can keep it.
steps.whatsHappening: A new objection against רבי יונתן begins. Here the גמרא only quotes the ברייתא; the punchline comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule is that a גזירה depends on the majority of the ציבור, not on every single person. The next step will show where this comes from, and that will hurt רבי יונתן.

keyTerms.meaning: They relied
A rabbinic decree
The community
Able to keep it, able to live with it

phrases.english: Rav Mesharshiya raised an objection:

phrases.aramaic: סָמְכוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ עַל דִּבְרֵי רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל
phrases.english: Our Sages relied on the words of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel

phrases.aramaic: וְעַל דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בְּרַבִּי צָדוֹק,
phrases.english: and on the words of Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Tzadok,
who would say:
We do not issue a decree upon the community
unless the majority of the community
is able to keep it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first challenges were answered, a new and stronger objection begins.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יונתן's reading of 'כל' as meaning every single one
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא bases a rule on the majority; the next step shows its source uses the word 'whole'.

steps.title: The פסוק says 'the whole nation' but means the majority
steps.stepSummary: רב אדא בר אבא brings the source: 'הגוי כלו', the whole nation. Since this 'whole' is read as 'most', 'all' in the Torah can mean 'most', against רבי יונתן.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב אדא בר אבא said: What is the source? 'You are cursed with the curse, yet you rob Me, the whole nation.' Here it is written 'the whole nation,' and still a majority is treated like the whole. This is a refutation of רבי יונתן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes רב משרשיא's objection. It shows a פסוק where 'whole' is read as 'most', which goes against רבי יונתן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יונתן said that writing 'all' must mean every single one. But in this פסוק, 'the whole nation' is used for a rule that depends only on the majority. So the word 'all' does not prove that every judge is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the פסוק? What is the source?
A curse
The whole nation
A majority is treated like the whole

steps.confusionAlert: Step 4 said the Torah usually treats a majority like the whole, so 'all' must mean every one. Here the גמרא turns this around: even where the Torah says 'whole', a majority still counts.

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַב אַדָּא בַּר אַבָּא: מַאי קְרָא?
phrases.english: And Rav Adda bar Abba said: What is the verse?
phrases.notes: He means: where do we learn the rule about decrees from?

phrases.english: "With the curse you are cursed,
yet you rob Me, the whole nation."
But here it is written "the whole nation,"
and still a majority is treated like the whole,
this is a refutation of Rabbi Yonatan.
phrases.notes: Some versions say יוחנן, in round brackets; the corrected wording is יונתן, in square brackets, the one from step 3.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַב אַדָּא בַּר אַבָּא: מַאי קְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source of the ברייתא from step 10 and completes the attack.
steps.raayaSupportSource: מלאכי 3:9, 'הגוי כלו', used for a rule that follows the majority

steps.title: רבי יונתן is refuted
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא accepts the objection: רבי יונתן's view is refuted.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a refutation.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא agrees that the objection works, and רבי יונתן's opinion is rejected.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No answer is given for רבי יונתן. So the idea that every single judge must rule is not accepted.

keyTerms.meaning: A refutation that stands; the opinion is rejected

steps.whatToRemember: The final view: 'all' in the Torah does not have to mean every single person. A majority can count as the whole, so רבי יונתן's view is rejected.

phrases.english: It is a refutation.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the refutation from step 11.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רבי יונתן is refuted; a court ruling does not need every single judge to agree.

steps.title: Then what does 'כל עדת' teach?
steps.stepSummary: Now that רבי יונתן is rejected, the גמרא asks what the words 'כל עדת' come to teach.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, what does 'the whole congregation' that the Torah says come to teach?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a question to set up the next step: if 'כל' does not mean every judge must agree, why does the Torah write it?
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יונתן's reading of 'כל עדת' was rejected. But the Torah's words must still teach something, so the גמרא looks for a new meaning.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, if so
The whole congregation (the פסוק about the court's mistaken ruling)
The Merciful One, meaning the Torah

phrases.english: Rather, what is "the whole congregation"
that the Merciful One says?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After rejecting רבי יונתן, asks for a new meaning of his source.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the words 'כל עדת' teach, if not that every judge must rule

steps.title: All the judges must be present
steps.stepSummary: 'כל עדת' means all the judges must be there. If they are, it is a court ruling; if not, it is not.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what it means: If all of them are there, it is a ruling. If not, it is not a ruling.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the new meaning of 'כל עדת': the whole court must be present.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'all' is about who is present, not about who agrees. When the full court is sitting, the majority decides and it counts as a ruling. If some judges are missing, it is not a court ruling at all.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it means
There is, they are present
It counts as a ruling

steps.whatToRemember: 'כל עדת' teaches that the full court must be present. Once they are all there, a majority vote is enough.
steps.whyThisMatters: This changes the meaning of 'all' from 'everyone agrees' to 'everyone is present', which fits with following the majority.

phrases.english: This is what it is saying:
if all of them are present, it is a ruling,
and if not, it is not a ruling.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 13.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'כל עדת' requires all the judges to be present; then the majority ruling counts.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A court ruling counts only when the full court is present.

steps.title: All judges on the court share the blame
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע teaches that when ten judges sit together, every one of them carries responsibility for the ruling.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע said: When ten judges sit together in judgment, the chain hangs on the neck of all of them.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע teaches that a ruling is the responsibility of every judge on the court, not just the leader.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 14 taught that all the judges must be present for a ruling to count as a court ruling. Now רבי יהושע adds the flip side: since all of them are part of it, all of them share the blame if it is wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: A chain or collar put on a condemned person; here it is a picture of responsibility for a ruling
Sitting in judgment as judges
Neck

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua said:
Ten who sit in judgment –
the chain hangs on the neck of all of them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a related teaching about the judges' shared responsibility after step 14 required all judges to be present
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Every judge who sits on a ruling shares full responsibility for it

steps.title: Isn't that obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבי יהושע needed to say this at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי יהושע. Of course everyone who rules is responsible, so why teach it? This sets up the next step's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge is that the statement seems to add nothing new. The גמרא expects every teaching to tell us something we would not have known.

keyTerms.meaning: It is obvious; a challenge that a statement teaches nothing new

phrases.english: It is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether רבי יהושע's statement in step 15 is needed
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהושע's statement that all judges are responsible
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: It is self-evident that everyone who takes part in a ruling is responsible, so the statement seems unnecessary

steps.title: Even a student before his teacher is responsible
steps.stepSummary: The new point is that even a student sitting with his teacher shares the blame, so he may not just stay quiet.
steps.simpleTranslation: This teaches us that even a student sitting before his teacher is responsible.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי יהושע is teaching something new. Even a student who sits with his own teacher is held responsible.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might have thought a student can rely on his רבי and stay quiet out of respect. רבי יהושע teaches that the student also carries the blame, so he must speak up if he sees a mistake.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it teaches us; the new point
A student in front of his teacher

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read this as 'the student is less guilty.' It means the opposite: he is not excused just because his רבי was there.

phrases.english: This teaches us
that even a student before his teacher (is responsible).
phrases.notes: The words in parentheses aren't in the Hebrew, but they're understood.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the פשיטא challenge of step 16
steps.terutzResolutionType: Identifies the new point (חידוש) in the statement
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A student sitting with his teacher could rely on the teacher and not be held responsible
steps.terutzMaskana: Even a student before his teacher carries responsibility for the ruling

steps.title: רב הונא brings ten scholars to share the load
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא would bring ten students of the study hall to court so that each would carry only a small piece of the responsibility.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רב הונא went out to court, he would bring ten תנאים from the study hall to sit before him, so that each of us would receive only a splinter from the beam.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story that shows רבי יהושע's idea in practice. רב הונא brought others into the court to share the responsibility.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since every judge shares responsibility, adding more judges spreads the weight. Each one carries only a small 'splinter' instead of the whole 'beam'.

keyTerms.meaning: Men in the study hall who recited משניות and ברייתות by heart
A splinter from the beam; a small share of a heavy load
The court

phrases.aramaic: רַב הוּנָא כִּי הֲוָה נָפֵיק לְבֵי דִינָא,
phrases.english: Rav Huna, when he would go out to the court,

phrases.aramaic: מַיְיתִי עֲשָׂרָה תַּנָּאֵי דְבֵי רַב לְקַמֵּיהּ,
phrases.english: would bring ten tanna'im of the study hall before him,
so that we will each receive a splinter from the beam.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב הוּנָא כִּי הֲוָה נָפֵיק לְבֵי דִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Illustrates the shared-responsibility principle of step 15 with a story
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A judge may bring more scholars to sit with him so the responsibility is shared

steps.title: רב אשי brings ten butchers for טריפה questions
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי did the same with questions about טריפות, bringing ten butchers from מתא מחסיא to sit before him.
steps.simpleTranslation: When they brought a טריפה question before רב אשי, he would bring ten butchers from מתא מחסיא and seat them before him. He said: so that each of us will receive a splinter from the beam.
steps.whatsHappening: A second story shows the same practice used for a different kind of ruling, a question about whether an animal is a טריפה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This shows the idea is not only for court cases. It applies to any halachic ruling a רב gives. The butchers were experienced with animals, so they were fitting partners in the decision.

keyTerms.meaning: An animal with a possible defect that might make it forbidden to eat
Butchers
The town where רב אשי lived and taught

steps.whatToRemember: Every judge shares the blame for a ruling, even a student. Great רבנים would bring others in to share that weight.

phrases.aramaic: רַב אָשֵׁי כִּי הֲווֹ מַיְיתִי טְרֵפְתָּא לְקַמֵּיהּ,
phrases.english: Rav Ashi, when they would bring a tereifa before him,
would bring ten butchers from Mata Mechasya
and seat them before him,

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר: כִּי הֵיכָא דְּנִימְטְיַין שִׁיבָּא מִכְּשׁוּרָא.
phrases.english: He said: so that we will each receive a splinter from the beam.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָשֵׁי כִּי הֲווֹ מַיְיתִי טְרֵפְתָּא לְקַמֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel story to step 18, extending the practice to ritual rulings about טריפות
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The practice of spreading responsibility applies to halachic rulings like טריפות as well

steps.title: New משנה: acting on a ruling the court already took back
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה discusses a person who acted on a court's mistaken ruling after the court had already reversed it. רבי שמעון exempts him and רבי אלעזר calls it a ספק.
steps.simpleTranslation: The court ruled, then realized it erred and took the ruling back, whether or not it had already brought its atonement offering. Someone then went and acted based on the old ruling. רבי שמעון exempts him. רבי אלעזר says it is a case of doubt.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It brings a case where someone sins by following a ruling that the court has already reversed, and two תנאים argue about his status.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The person relied on the court, but the ruling was no longer in force when he acted. רבי שמעון treats him as fully exempt from a קרבן. רבי אלעזר says his status is doubtful, so he brings an אשם תלוי, the offering for a doubtful sin.

keyTerms.meaning: The court issued a ruling
They reversed themselves; took back the ruling
Their atonement offering for the mistaken ruling
Based on their word; following their ruling
Doubt; here it means he brings an אָשָׁם תָּלוּי

phrases.english: MISHNA: The court issued a ruling
and they realized that they erred and reversed themselves,
whether they brought their atonement offering
or whether they did not bring their atonement offering,
and someone went and acted based on their (first) ruling –
Rabbi Shimon exempts him,
and Rabbi Elazar says: it is a doubt.
phrases.notes: A 'doubt' here means he brings an אשם תלוי, the offering brought when you are not sure you sinned.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ הוֹרוּ בֵּית דִּין וְיָדְעוּ שֶׁטָּעוּ וְחָזְרוּ בָּהֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new משנה and a new topic
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Someone who acts on a ruling the court already reversed is exempt according to רבי שמעון, and in doubt (אשם תלוי) according to רבי אלעזר

steps.title: Which case counts as a doubt?
steps.stepSummary: The משנה asks which situation רבי אלעזר means by 'doubt'.
steps.simpleTranslation: Which is the case of doubt?
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה asks a clarifying question about רבי אלעזר's word 'doubt'. This sets up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Doubt' is vague. The משנה wants to define exactly when the person is treated as in doubt and when he is not.

keyTerms.meaning: Which is; asks for a definition

phrases.english: Which is the case of doubt?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the definition of רבי אלעזר's term in step 20
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What situation counts as the 'doubt' case

steps.title: At home he is liable; overseas he is exempt
steps.stepSummary: If he stayed home, he is liable. If he went overseas, he is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he sat in his house, he is liable. If he went away to a far-off land overseas, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה answers the question. The person who stayed home is liable, and the person who traveled far away is exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The difference depends on whether he could have heard that the court reversed itself. At home he could have found out, so he is liable for the doubt offering. Far away he had no way to know, so he is exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: Liable; here, to bring the doubt offering
Exempt
A land overseas; a far-away place

phrases.english: If he sat inside his house – he is liable,
if he went away to a land overseas – he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 21
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Staying home makes him liable (doubt offering); being overseas makes him exempt

steps.title: רבי עקיבא agrees about the one overseas
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא says he agrees that the one who went overseas is closer to being exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי עקיבא said: I agree in this case that he is closer to exemption than to liability.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי עקיבא gives his view on the overseas case. He agrees that this person leans toward being exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי עקיבא accepts the exemption for the one who traveled away, but in careful words: he is 'closer to' exemption. This leads בן עזאי to ask why this case is different from staying home.

keyTerms.meaning: I agree; I concede
Closer to exemption
Obligation; liability

phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva said:
I agree in this case
phrases.notes: 'This case' is the one who went overseas.

phrases.english: that he is closer to exemption than to liability.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא: מוֹדֶה אֲנִי בָּזֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: רבי עקיבא responds to the overseas case of step 22
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The one who went overseas is closer to exemption than liability

steps.title: בן עזאי asks: why is he different?
steps.stepSummary: בן עזאי challenges רבי עקיבא: what makes the traveler different from the one who stayed home?
steps.simpleTranslation: בן עזאי said to him: How is this one different from the one who sits in his house?
steps.whatsHappening: בן עזאי challenges רבי עקיבא's distinction between the two people. This sets up רבי עקיבא's explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both people followed the court's old ruling in the same way. בן עזאי wants to know why the place where each one was should change the law.

keyTerms.meaning: What is different; how is this case unlike that one

phrases.english: Ben Azzai said to him:

phrases.aramaic: מַאי שְׁנָא זֶה מִן הַיּוֹשֵׁב בְּבֵיתוֹ?
phrases.english: How is this one different from one who sits in his house?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי שְׁנָא זֶה מִן הַיּוֹשֵׁב בְּבֵיתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the distinction רבי עקיבא accepted in step 23
steps.kashyaTarget: The distinction between the one at home and the one overseas
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Both acted on the same ruling, so it is unclear why their location should change the law

steps.title: The one at home could have heard
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא explains that the one at home could have heard the court changed its ruling, but the one overseas could not.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because the one who sits at home could have heard, but this one could not have heard.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי עקיבא answers בן עזאי. The difference is whether the person had a chance to hear that the court reversed its ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Liability depends on whether he could have known. The one at home was near enough to hear the news, so he carries some blame. The traveler had no real way to find out, so he is closer to exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: Possible
That he would hear

steps.whatToRemember: A person who follows a ruling the court already reversed is judged by whether he could have heard about the reversal. At home he could have heard, so he is liable. Overseas he could not, so he is exempt.

phrases.english: For the one who sits in his house
phrases.notes: This is רבי עקיבא answering, even though the text does not say his name again.

phrases.english: it would have been possible for him to hear,

phrases.aramaic: וְזֶה לֹא הָיָה לוֹ אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיִּשְׁמַע.
phrases.english: but this one could not possibly have heard.

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁהַיּוֹשֵׁב בְּבֵיתוֹ אֶפְשָׁר הָיָה לוֹ שֶׁיִּשְׁמַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers בן עזאי's challenge in step 24
steps.terutzResolutionType: Identifies a real difference between the cases
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both people are the same since both followed the court's ruling
steps.terutzMaskana: The one at home could have learned of the reversal while the traveler could not, so their status differs

steps.title: Uprooting a whole מצוה is exempt, cancelling part is liable
steps.stepSummary: The משנה states the rule. If בית דין rules that a whole מצוה is not in the תורה, the court is פטור. If it cancels only part of a מצוה, the court is חייב.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the court ruled to uproot an entire מצוה, for example by saying "there is no נדה in the תורה," "there is no שבת in the תורה," or "there is no עבודה זרה in the תורה," they are exempt. If they ruled to cancel part and keep part, they are liable.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה sets out two kinds of mistaken court rulings: wiping out a whole מצוה, and cutting away just one piece of it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wiping out a whole מצוה that everyone knows is in the תורה is not treated as a real ruling, so the court is פטור. Cancelling only one detail is the kind of mistaken ruling that makes the court חייב to bring a קרבן.

keyTerms.meaning: They ruled (gave a halachic decision)
To uproot the entire body (the whole essence) of a מצוה
To cancel part and keep part
Exempt (no קרבן required)
Liable (must bring a קרבן)

steps.confusionAlert: It seems backwards that the bigger mistake (uprooting everything) is פטור. The court is not let off for a small error. A ruling that the whole מצוה is missing is not counted as a ruling at all.

phrases.aramaic: הוֹרוּ בֵּית דִּין לַעֲקוֹר אֶת כָּל הַגּוּף,
phrases.english: If the court ruled to uproot the entire essence of a מצוה,
for example, they said: there is no prohibition of a menstruating woman in the Torah,
there is no Shabbat in the Torah,
there is no prohibition of idol worship in the Torah,
then these are exempt.
If they ruled to cancel part of a מצוה and keep part,
then these are liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: הוֹרוּ בֵּית דִּין לַעֲקוֹר אֶת כָּל הַגּוּף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic. The earlier steps dealt with someone who acted on a court ruling. This step asks what kind of ruling makes the court itself liable.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Uprooting a whole מצוה makes the court פטור. Cancelling part of a מצוה makes the court חייב.

steps.title: How does cancelling part of a מצוה look?
steps.stepSummary: The משנה asks for a concrete example of "cancelling part and keeping part."
steps.simpleTranslation: How so?
steps.whatsHappening: This is a short setup question. The משנה is getting ready to show examples of a partial cancellation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: "Cancel part, keep part" is abstract. The question asks what such a ruling actually sounds like.

keyTerms.meaning: How so? (asks for an example)

phrases.english: How so?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for examples of the second half of the rule in step 26.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A concrete example of a ruling that cancels part of a מצוה while keeping the rest.

steps.title: Three examples of cancelling one detail
steps.stepSummary: The examples are נדה, שבת and עבודה זרה. Each time the court admits the מצוה exists but frees one specific act. In such cases the court is חייב.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: there is נדה in the תורה, but one who lives with a woman who is a שומרת יום כנגד יום is exempt. There is שבת in the תורה, but one who carries from a private domain to a public domain is exempt. There is עבודה זרה in the תורה, but one who bows is exempt. These are liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה answers "how so" with three cases. In each one the court keeps the מצוה but wrongly says one act is allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These are the same three מצוות from step 26, now with only a single detail removed. Because the מצוה itself is admitted and just one part is cut away, this counts as a real mistaken ruling. That is why the court is חייב.

keyTerms.meaning: A woman who keeps a clean day in exchange for a day she saw blood
One who carries out an object
Private domain / public domain
One who bows down (to an idol)

phrases.english: They said: there is a prohibition of a menstruating woman in the Torah,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל הַבָּא עַל שׁוֹמֶרֶת יוֹם כְּנֶגֶד יוֹם – פָּטוּר,
phrases.english: but one who lives with a woman who keeps a day for a day is exempt,
phrases.notes: This is a woman who saw blood outside her regular time and must wait a clean day before she becomes permitted.

phrases.english: there is Shabbat in the Torah,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל הַמּוֹצִיא מֵרְשׁוּת הַיָּחִיד לִרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים – פָּטוּר,
phrases.english: but one who carries from a private domain to a public domain is exempt,
there is idol worship in the Torah,
but one who bows to an idol is exempt,
in these cases they are liable,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the כיצד question of step 27.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Admitting a מצוה exists but freeing one act within it, such as carrying on שבת or bowing to an idol, is a partial cancellation that makes the court חייב.

steps.title: Proof from the verse: "a matter," not the whole
steps.stepSummary: The משנה proves its rule from the פסוק "ונעלם דבר." Liability comes when a "matter" (one detail) is hidden, not the whole מצוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says: "And a matter is hidden." A matter, and not the entire essence.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives the source in the תורה for the whole rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says a "דבר," a matter, was hidden from the court. That word points to one piece of a מצוה being hidden, not the entire מצוה. This explains both halves of step 26: a partial error makes the court חייב, and uprooting everything makes it פטור.

keyTerms.meaning: "And a matter is hidden" (the פסוק about a court's mistaken ruling)
As it is said (introduces a פסוק)

steps.whatToRemember: A court brings a קרבן only for an error in a detail of a מצוה. Ruling that a whole מצוה does not exist makes the court פטור, because the פסוק says "דבר," a matter, and not the whole body of the מצוה.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the basic boundary of הוראת בית דין: only a partial, believable mistake counts as the kind of ruling the תורה deals with.

phrases.english: as it is stated: "And a matter is hidden":
a matter, and not the entire essence.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source in the תורה for the rule of step 26 and the examples of step 28.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that the court is חייב only for cancelling part of a מצוה, not for uprooting all of it.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ויקרא 4:13, "ונעלם דבר": the word "דבר" means one detail, not the whole.

steps.title: רב's reason for רבי שמעון: he acted with the court's permission
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins. רב יהודה quotes רב, who explains that רבי שמעון exempts the person because he acted with the permission of the בית דין.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: What is רבי שמעון's reason? Since he is acting with the permission of the בית דין.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts its discussion of the משנה by asking why רבי שמעון exempts someone who followed the court's ruling even after the court changed its mind. רב answers that the person was acting with the court's permission.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, the court took back its ruling, but this person still did the act based on the first ruling. רב explains that רבי שמעון sees him as still covered by the court's permission, so he is פטור.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the reason?
Since / because
With the permission of the court

phrases.english: Gemara:
Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
What is the reason of Rabbi Shimon?

phrases.aramaic: הוֹאִיל וּבִרְשׁוּת בֵּית דִּין הוּא עוֹשֶׂה.
phrases.english: Since he acts with the permission of the court.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא on the משנה's argument about someone who acted after the court took back its ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי שמעון exempts the person because he acted with the court's permission.

steps.title: Second version: a ruling is only there to tell apart unknowing and knowing sins
steps.stepSummary: Another version of רב's words: according to רבי שמעון, any ruling that spread to most of the community exempts the individual who follows it. The court's ruling decides whether his act counts as שוגג or מזיד.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: רבי שמעון used to say: Any ruling that went out to most of the community, an individual who acts on it is exempt. A ruling is only given to tell the difference between שוגג and מזיד.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second version of what רב said about רבי שמעון. Once a ruling has spread to most of the people, an individual who follows it is פטור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This version adds a condition: the ruling must have spread to most of the community. The reason given is that a court ruling is what marks a person's act as שוגג instead of מזיד. Someone who acts relying on such a ruling counts as שוגג.

keyTerms.meaning: The majority of the community
An individual
Doing something wrong without knowing
Doing something wrong on purpose

steps.confusionAlert: Both versions are from רב, quoted by רב יהודה. They are not two different אמוראים arguing. It is the same teaching remembered in two ways.

phrases.aramaic: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב,
phrases.english: Some say: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said,
Rabbi Shimon would say:
Any ruling that went out to the majority of the community,
an individual who acts on it is exempt,
because a ruling was given only
to distinguish between unwitting and intentional acts.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second version of רב's explanation of רבי שמעון.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A ruling that spread to most of the community exempts the individual who follows it, because the ruling makes his act שוגג.

steps.title: Challenge: a special collection for the offerings makes the mistake known
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says that according to רבי שמעון, money for the פר העלם דבר and the שעירי עבודה זרה is collected specially. A special collection would tell everyone the court made a mistake, so why is the person still exempt?
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged: For the bull of a hidden matter of the community and the goats for עבודה זרה, a new collection is made for them from the start. These are the words of רבי שמעון. רבי יהודה says: They come from the Temple chamber funds. Why then is he exempt? Since money is collected for them, the sin has become known to him!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to challenge רבי שמעון's view. If everyone gives money specially for these offerings, then everyone knows the court made a mistake. That should make the person liable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי שמעון holds that a fresh collection is made just for these communal sin offerings. A collection like that would spread the news that the court's ruling was wrong. So the person now knows, which is "הודע", and should not count as relying on the court.

keyTerms.meaning: The bull brought when the community sinned following a mistaken court ruling
The goats brought for a communal mistake about idol worship
The general Temple fund from the yearly half-shekel
"It was made known". The sin became known to him.

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
The bull for an unwitting sin of the community
and the goats for idol worship,
they collect money for them from the start,
these are the words of Rabbi Shimon.
Rabbi Yehuda says:
They come from the funds of the Temple chamber.
Why is he exempt? Since they collect for them,
it is for him "it became known"!
phrases.notes: This is the Torah's word for a sinner learning of his sin (ויקרא 4:28).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי שמעון's exemption by using his own view about collecting money.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's explanation (steps 30–31) of why רבי שמעון exempts the person who acted after the court took back its ruling.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי שמעון himself holds that money is specially collected for these offerings. That makes the court's mistake public, so the person should know and be liable.

steps.title: First answer: the money was collected without saying what it was for
steps.stepSummary: The collection was made without saying what it was for, so the person did not learn that the court had made a mistake.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, say: it is a case where they collected without saying what it was for.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The money was collected without saying what it was for, so nobody learned about the mistake from it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge assumed the collection announced the court's error. If the collection was "סתם", with no reason given, it tells people nothing. So the person still did not know, and רבי שמעון can still exempt him.

keyTerms.meaning: If you want, say (introduces a possible answer)
Without saying what it was for

phrases.english: If you wish, say:
For example, where they collected without specifying.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by limiting the case to a collection that gave no reason.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The special collection tells everyone that the court made a mistake.
steps.terutzMaskana: The collection was made without a stated reason, so the person did not find out.

steps.title: Second answer: the person was not in town
steps.stepSummary: Another answer: the person was not in the city during the collection, so he never heard about it.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say: it is a case where he was not in the city.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second answer. Even if the collection was announced, this person was away from the city and did not hear about it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answer accepts that the collection may have announced the mistake. But it only makes the mistake known to people who were there. Someone out of town still relied on the court without knowing, so he stays פטור.

keyTerms.meaning: Town / city

steps.whatToRemember: רבי שמעון exempts someone who follows a court ruling as long as he did not know the court took it back. A special collection does not change this if no reason was given, or if he was out of town.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
For example, where he was not in the city.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, separate answer to the same challenge.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Everyone hears about the collection and learns about the mistake.
steps.terutzMaskana: This person was out of town, so he did not hear and remained שוגג.

steps.title: רב follows the version of the ברייתא with the opinions reversed
steps.stepSummary: A third answer: רב holds like a ברייתא that switches the opinions. In that version רבי שמעון says the offerings are paid from the Temple chamber's funds, so there is no special collection at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you can say: רב follows the other תנא, who teaches the opinions the other way around. רבי יהודה says the money is collected from the start, and רבי שמעון says the offerings are paid from the chamber's funds.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another answer to the question from Step 32. It says that רב relies on a different ברייתא in which רבי שמעון holds there is no special collection.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The קשיא was that a special collection would tell everyone that the court made a mistake. In this reversed ברייתא, רבי שמעון says the money comes from funds that are already in the Temple treasury. Nothing is publicly collected, so the person could easily not know about the court's mistake, and רבי שמעון can still exempt him.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish, say: introduces another possible answer
The other תנא, a different teacher of the ברייתא
The reverse: the opinions are switched
The funds already collected into the Temple treasury chamber

steps.confusionAlert: In this ברייתא the opinions are swapped. Here it is רבי יהודה who says there is a special collection, and רבי שמעון who says the money comes from the chamber.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
Rav holds like the other tanna,
as it is taught the other way around:
phrases.notes: This is the same argument as the ברייתא in Step 32, but with the two names switched.

phrases.english: From the outset they collect money for them,
these are the words of Rabbi Yehuda.
Rabbi Shimon says:
They come from the collection of the Temple chamber.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: רַב כְּאִידַּךְ תַּנָּא סָבַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third answer to the קשיא of Step 32, alongside the answers in Steps 33 and 34.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Switching to a different version of the source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי שמעון requires a special public collection, which would tell everyone about the court's mistake.
steps.terutzMaskana: In the version רב follows, רבי שמעון takes the money from existing chamber funds, so nothing is announced.
steps.whatToRemember: There are three answers to the collection question: the collection did not say what it was for, the person was out of town, or רב follows the reversed ברייתא where רבי שמעון has no collection at all.

steps.title: Four opinions about someone who followed the ruling after the court took it back
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא lists four views. רבי מאיר says he is liable, רבי שמעון says he is exempt, רבי אלעזר says his case is a ספק, and סומכוס says his case is left hanging.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: רבי מאיר holds him liable, and רבי שמעון exempts him. רבי אלעזר says it is a doubt. In the name of סומכוס they said: it is hanging.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a related ברייתא. It deals with a person who acted on the court's original ruling after the court had already taken it back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר says he must bring a חטאת, and רבי שמעון exempts him because he relied on the court. רבי אלעזר and סומכוס both stand in the middle and treat his status as uncertain. The גמרא has not yet said how their two views differ, and that sets up the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Holds him liable to bring a חטאת
Exempts him
A doubt or uncertainty
Hanging, undecided

phrases.english: It was taught: Rabbi Meir holds him liable,
phrases.notes: The case is a person who acted on the court's ruling after the court had already taken it back.

phrases.english: and Rabbi Shimon exempts him,
Rabbi Elazar says: it is a doubt,
in the name of Sumakhos they said: it is hanging.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a related ברייתא on the same topic of following a court ruling that the court has taken back.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There are four views: liable (רבי מאיר), exempt (רבי שמעון), a doubt (רבי אלעזר), and hanging (סומכוס).

steps.title: The difference between רבי אלעזר and סומכוס is the אשם תלוי
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן explains that the practical difference between 'a doubt' and 'hanging' is whether the person brings an אשם תלוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: The difference between them is an אשם תלוי.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן explains how the two middle opinions really differ. 'ספק' and 'תלוי' sound alike, but they have different results.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רבי אלעזר, the person's case counts as a real ספק, so he brings an אשם תלוי the way anyone who is unsure whether he sinned would. According to סומכוס, the question is simply left open and he brings nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: A provisional guilt-offering, brought when a person is unsure whether he sinned
There is a difference between them

steps.confusionAlert: Both opinions sound like 'unsure,' but only רבי אלעזר's ספק requires an offering. סומכוס's תלוי means he brings nothing.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
A provisional guilt-offering is the difference between them.
phrases.notes: Between them means between רבי אלעזר and סומכוס, the two in-between views.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the practical difference between two of the opinions in Step 36.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי אלעזר requires an אשם תלוי. סומכוס does not.

steps.title: רבי זירא's comparison explaining רבי אלעזר
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא compares רבי אלעזר's case to a person who ate fat that might be forbidden חלב and might be permitted שומן. When he finds out about the doubt, he brings an אשם תלוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא said: What is רבי אלעזר's view like? It is like a person who ate fat that might be חלב and might be שומן, and then he found out. He brings an אשם תלוי.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא gives a comparison to show why רבי אלעזר requires an אשם תלוי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone who ate fat and later learned it might have been forbidden חלב brings an אשם תלוי because he is unsure whether he sinned. In the same way, when this person learns the court took back its ruling, it is unclear whether he acted because he relied on the court or on his own. That uncertainty makes his case a real ספק.

keyTerms.meaning: A comparison or analogy
To what is this comparable?
Forbidden fat, which carries כרת if eaten on purpose
Permitted fat
And he found out

steps.whatToRemember: רבי אלעזר treats the person like anyone who might have sinned without knowing it. Because there is a real doubt, he brings an אשם תלוי, just as in the case of fat that might be חלב.

phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira said:
A comparison for the view of Rabbi Elazar:
To what is the matter comparable?
To a person who ate
something that might be forbidden fat and might be permitted fat,
and he found out, who brings a guilt-offering.
phrases.notes: He found out about the doubt itself. The offering here is the אשם תלוי from the previous step.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָשָׁל דְּרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר לָמָּה הַדָּבָר דּוֹמֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a comparison to explain why רבי אלעזר requires the אשם תלוי mentioned in Step 37.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Following a retracted ruling is like eating fat that might be חלב. There is a real doubt about whether he sinned, so he brings an אשם תלוי.
